body.text: Africa’s richest man, Aliko Dangote, is building a 700,000-barrels-per-day (bpd) oil refinery in Lamu Port in Kenya on the Indian Ocean shores. Once completed, it offers Australia a chance to diversify its oil supplies west of the Indian Ocean.

The conflict in the Middle East and the subsequent supply chain disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz exposed Australia’s fuel vulnerabilities, driving energy prices higher. While Australia is a major net exporter of energy, driven largely by its exports of thermal coal and liquefied natural gas (LNG), it is a net importer of oil, relying heavily on overseas supplies of refined products including diesel, petrol, and jet fuel, mainly from Singapore, South Korea and Malaysia. These Asian refiners obtain their crude oil mainly from the Middle East, and the conflict in the region has recently affected their production. In 2023, for example, Australia exported 94% of its crude products (oil, condensate and liquefied petroleum gas) and imported about 90% of its oil requirements.

Although Australia is ramping up domestic exploration, reliance on overseas supplies will continue for now. Asian neighbours will undoubtedly remain Australia’s largest oil suppliers, but the Iran war showed there is room for Australia to look for alternative sources before the next crisis.

Most of Australia’s current suppliers are also located within a highly contested Indo-Pacific. The South China Sea and the Taiwan Strait remain vulnerable maritime routes, and a potential blockage could disrupt Australia’s petroleum supplies. Australia urgently needs alternatives.

The Dangote East Africa Refinery will cost upwards of US$16 billion, with the aim to be completed around 2030. It will use Kenya’s oil production and potentially that of other countries in the region, including South Sudan, Angola, Nigeria, and Uganda. A groundbreaking ceremony for the refinery took place on 30 September 2026, with Dangote having moved massive amounts of machinery to Lamu to begin work. The Dangote group would have a 70% stake in the refinery, and the remaining 30% to be shared by countries in the region.

An East African energy corridor is emerging. On the same western Indian Ocean coastline, just below the Kenya–Tanzania border, sits Tanga Port (located in Tanzania), where the 1,447-kilometre East Africa Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) terminates. This pipeline, estimated to have a peak capacity of 246,000 bpd, is now at 93% completion and will transport Uganda’s crude oil from Kabaale in Hoima to Tanga for export to international markets. Uganda is also building its own small refinery capable of processing about 60,000 bpd.
The objective is not to build Australia's future around African oil, but to explore additional Indian Ocean supply options while reducing fossil-fuel dependence.

The arrival of Dangote in the Kenyan energy sector supports Nairobi’s long-conceived dream of creating a developmental corridor, the Lamu Port-South Sudan-Ethiopia Transport (LAPSSET) Corridor, which features several cross-border connectivity projects, including ports, pipelines, highways, and rail lines, and aims to open the landlocked region to business and development. While the logistical arrangements for transporting crude oil from other African producers, including South Sudan, Angola, and West African countries, to the refinery remain uncertain, Uganda’s crude oil can be transported relatively efficiently from Tanga to Lamu. Kenya’s crude oil resources from the Lokichar Basin in the northern part of the country are expected to supply feedstock to the proposed Lamu refinery.

Australia should pay attention for three main reasons. First, for diversification. East Africa will offer Australia as another source of petroleum supply in addition to its current concentration in Asia. Australia has recently been forced to look as far as Canada to offset the fuel crisis. If East African oil starts flowing, this would be a much closer and potentially cheaper option.

Second, Lamu and Tanga sit within Australia’s broader Indian Ocean strategic environment. Western Australia not only faces the Indian Ocean but is also Australia’s closest major geographic region to East Africa (just under 10,000 kilometres). Australia recognises the significance of the Indian Ocean, and yet “barely looks West”, paying more attention to the Pacific. An oil hub growing along the shores of the Indian Ocean offers a reason to shift view.

Finally, for economic diplomacy, Australia should strengthen relations with Africa, starting with littoral states such as Kenya and Tanzania, which serve as gateways to the interior. Australia could engage early in Africa’s emerging energy markets rather than arriving after the infrastructure has already been built. Dangote Group’s Nigeria-based facility – the largest refinery in Africa and the world’s 7th largest – has become Europe’s largest supplier of jet fuel, overtaking American suppliers. Africa also matters to Australia’s campaign to win a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council in 2029.

First, although Western Australia offers a potential entry point for East African petroleum, the closure of the Kwinana refinery means any opportunity would depend on import-terminal capacity, distribution infrastructure and the commercial viability of supplying refineries, such as Geelong on the other side of the country.

Second, energy security must be balanced against the clean-energy transition. While liquid fuels will remain essential to several sectors, potential East African supply arrangements must be assessed against likely demand, emissions and commercial viability. The objective is not to build Australia’s future around African oil, but to explore additional Indian Ocean supply options while reducing fossil-fuel dependence.
